Adsorbent / material: Synthetic goethite (α-FeOOH), BET surface area 63.53 m²/g; mean particle size 3.04 µm; PZC ~8.2
Experimental design / conditions: 20 mg goethite in 10 mL (2 g/L); initial TC 50 mg/L (0.1125 mM); 150 rpm; 25 ± 0.5 °C; kinetic study; later studies equilibrated 24 h. The main-text method gives this setup.
Reported result: Over 80% of sorption occurred during the first 4 h. Pseudo-second-order fitted equilibrium loading qe = 14.71 mg/g; initial rate = 9.80 mg g−1 h−1; rate constant k = 0.045 g mg−1 h−1; reported fit R² = 0.999.
Value / units: 14.71 mg/g fitted qe; 9.80 mg g−1 h−1; k = 0.045 g mg−1 h−1
Model / metric: Pseudo-second-order kinetic fit; qe is a fitted kinetic parameter, not a saturation/isotherm qmax
Caveat / follow-up: Goethite is a synthetic iron oxyhydroxide, not a natural clay or carbon adsorbent; use for mechanism/solution-chemistry synthesis rather than core cross-class performance rankings. Do not infer Q1 eligibility before ranking audit.

Experimental design / conditions: TC initial concentration 0.1125 mM (50 mg/L); pH 3–10; background electrolyte cations Li+, Na+, K+, Ca2+ or Mg2+ at 0.01 M; 2.0 g/L goethite; 25 °C; equilibration time 24 h.
Reported result: TC adsorption increased from about 10 mmol kg−1 at pH 3 to about 22 mmol kg−1 at pH 8; the five background electrolyte cations showed little discernible effect over the studied pH range.
Value / units: ~10 to ~22 mmol kg−1 goethite, as shown/reported
Model / metric: Observed adsorption-edge result in Figure 4; units as printed by source
Caveat / follow-up: Authors interpret TC–goethite binding as mainly inner-sphere surface complexation; background cations mainly form weaker outer-sphere complexes. They note Ca2+/Mg2+ solution ionic strength was three times that of Li+/Na+/K+ solutions. Keep this system distinct from clay cation-exchange data.

Experimental design / conditions: TC 0.1125 mM; 0.01 M NaNO3 background electrolyte; goethite 2.0 g/L; 25 °C; 24 h; Cu(II) concentrations 0.008, 0.040 and 0.100 mM; pH varied.
Reported result: At pH 5.5, TC adsorption increased from 16.2 mmol kg−1 without Cu(II) to 30.4, 40.0 and 49.0 mmol kg−1 as Cu(II) increased to 0.008, 0.040 and 0.100 mM, respectively.
Caveat / follow-up: Authors propose Cu(II) acts as a bridge between goethite and TC through a ternary surface complex; this is an interpretation, not direct proof of every complex species. Do not generalise to all divalent cations.

Experimental design / conditions: HA concentrations 5, 50 and 100 mg/L in 0.01 M NaNO3; goethite 2.0 g/L; 25 °C; 24 h; pH varied.
Reported result: HA significantly increased TC adsorption at pH < 7, with maximum sorption around pH 4.3; larger increases occurred at higher HA concentration. At pH > 7, HA produced only a slight enhancement.

Adsorbent / material: Ordered mesoporous carbon CMK-3 (OMC) and bamboo-based carbon (BC), each before and after ammonia treatment
Experimental design / conditions: OMC prepared by SBA-15 silica templating and furfuryl-alcohol carbon precursor with high-temperature carbonization; BC starts from commercial bamboo charcoal, washed/dried and pyrolysed at 500 °C for 3 h under N2, then phosphoric-acid impregnated at 1:1 ratio, dried at 200 °C for 24 h and washed to near-neutral pH. Both OMC and BC were ammonia-treated at 1173 K (~900 °C) for 1 h after N2 pretreatment at 573 K (~300 °C) for 3 h.
Reported result: BET area (m²/g): virgin BC 509; modified BC 767; virgin OMC 1181; modified OMC 1746. Total pore volume (cm³/g): 0.31; 0.36; 1.04; 1.46. Average pore diameter (nm): 2.36; 1.87; 3.2; 3.7, respectively. pHPZC: 7.6; 8.5; 7.9; 8.8.
Value / units: BET m²/g; pore volume cm³/g; pore diameter nm; pHPZC values
Model / metric: Characterization values reported in Table 1 and §3.1; four carbon conditions
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2–4 (printed pp. 350–352), §§2.2–2.5, Table 1, Tables 2–4 and Fig. 7
Caveat / follow-up: Important classification caveat: the paper's 'virgin BC' had already undergone phosphoric-acid impregnation (1:1) and 500 °C pyrolysis before its later ammonia modification comparison. It is not untreated/raw bamboo charcoal. OMC is a templated engineered carbon, not a low-processing feedstock char.

Adsorbent / material: Virgin BC; modified BC; virgin OMC; modified OMC

Adsorbent / material: Virgin BC; modified BC; virgin OMC; modified OMC
Experimental design / conditions: pH varied from 2 to 12; initial CIP concentration 200 mg/L; 0.03 g adsorbent; 25 °C, according to §3.6. pHPZC values reported as 7.6, 8.5, 7.9 and 8.8 for virgin BC, modified BC, virgin OMC and modified OMC.

Model / metric: Observed pH-edge/capacity values as reported; pH/speciation interpretation

Adsorbent / material: Virgin BC; modified BC; virgin OMC; modified OMC
Experimental design / conditions: Temperature tests at 25, 35 and 45 °C, shaker 120 rpm for 24 h. NaCl tests used 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 1 mol/L; the method states 0.03 g adsorbent and 50 mL of 200 mg/L CIP solution in 100-mL flasks.
Reported result: Adsorption capacity increased as temperature rose from 25 to 45 °C. With NaCl, reported sorption increased markedly as concentration rose from 0 to 0.2 M, changed less through 0.5 M and approached a plateau between 0.5 and 1 M; authors attribute this mainly to a salting-out effect.
Value / units: Qualitative temperature/salt trend; no harmonised single capacity value transcribed
Model / metric: Observed experimental trend and authors' mechanistic interpretation
Caveat / follow-up: Very high NaCl concentrations (up to 1 M) are mechanistic laboratory conditions, not representative of most environmental waters. No real-water/column/cost evidence identified in the uploaded main PDF.

Adsorbent / material: Bagasse biochar variants: pristine PBC; additional-pyrolysis BC; acetone-washed BCA; nitric-acid-washed BCN
Experimental design / conditions: PBC prepared from washed/dried/ground bagasse by pyrolysis under N2 at 350 °C for 1 h. BC: PBC water-washed and pyrolysed at 950 °C for 3 h. Main text reports BET area of BCA/BCN in the range 1044.41–1119.53 m²/g and pore volume 1.26–1.36 cm³/g; it cites Supplementary Table S1.

Value / units: BET area 1044.41–1119.53 m²/g; pore volume 1.26–1.36 cm³/g (BCA/BCN range reported in main text)
Model / metric: Material preparation and physicochemical characterization; BET values refer to SI Table S1

Evidence status: Full text checked; key supplementary source not uploaded

Adsorbent / material: Primarily BCA and BCN for solution-matrix experiments
Evidence domain: Humic acid and real-water matrix effects
Experimental design / conditions: HA concentrations 0.05–1.0 g/L. Freshwater from FuRong Lake and seawater from Baicheng Beach were filtered through 0.22-µm nylon fibre before analysis. Reported TOC values: ultrapure water 0.8827, seawater 5.518 and freshwater 4.163 mg/L.
Reported result: HA and real-water matrices reduced SMX adsorption capacity by more than half but slightly enhanced TC adsorption. SMX capacity in seawater and freshwater was much lower than in ultrapure water; the paper associates this with higher TOC. TC adsorption increased slightly in natural-water matrices, which authors link to soluble organic matter/π–π interactions.
Value / units: Qualitative relative effects; TOC 0.8827 / 5.518 / 4.163 mg/L for UW / sea / fresh water
Model / metric: Observed matrix-effect comparison; authors' mechanism is interpretive
Caveat / follow-up: These are filtered freshwater and seawater matrices, not municipal wastewater effluent. The main paper's solutions are adsorption test solutions; do not describe this as removal of native antibiotic contamination from the lake/seawater.

Experimental design / conditions: Reusability evaluated in four continuous loops. Group A underwent no regeneration treatment; Group B biochar was washed with 80% methanol, 15% acetone and 5% acetic acid before reuse.
Reported result: After four cycles, the no-regeneration Group A adsorption capacity decreased by no more than 5%. For regenerated Group B, fourth-cycle removal efficiencies were reported as BCA: 23.52% (SMX) and 29.87% (TC); BCN: 29.73% (SMX) and 32.11% (TC).
Value / units: Capacity loss ≤5% in Group A; fourth-cycle removal efficiencies as reported for Group B
Model / metric: Four-cycle reuse test; regeneration solvent blend differs from untreated reuse
Caveat / follow-up: Do not conflate the Group A capacity-loss result with Group B removal efficiency. Do not infer percent capacity retained or desorption efficiency unless SI/figures define it explicitly. Organic solvent regeneration requires recovery and spent-solvent consideration.

Experimental design / conditions: XPS/FTIR characterization after adsorption; main paper refers to SI for additional kinetics/isotherm fit details. Adsorption tests are batch tests.
Reported result: Authors attribute SMX adsorption partly to O-containing groups (e.g., C–O/C–O–C) and TC adsorption to O-functional-group complexation and π–π interaction. Pore filling contributes but is described as not dominant. Authors explicitly note that column studies with different natural waters are needed for scale-up and that the soluble-organic-matter enhancement of TC needs further study.
Value / units: Qualitative mechanism interpretation; no harmonised mechanistic contribution percentage
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 5 and 8–9, Fig. 4, Fig. 10, §§3.2.4 and 4 Conclusions
Evidence status: Full text checked; SI not supplied; source limitations preserved
Caveat / follow-up: Mechanisms inferred from spectroscopy and adsorption behaviour; do not describe every proposed interaction as conclusively proven. Study reports no column validation or cost/LCA in the main PDF.
